memoryText: And in the wilderness, where you saw how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went until you came to this place.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Deuteronomy 1:31 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Deuteronomy 1:31 is a single sentence, spoken at the end of a forty-year journey, that changes how we look at the whole wilderness.

“In the wilderness.” The wilderness is the place of testing and failure in the Bible. It is where Israel grumbled, rebelled, and wandered. Moses does not deny any of it. But he tells them to look again.

“Where you saw how the LORD your God carried you.” The people had seen many things in the wilderness: manna, water from the rock, fire and cloud. Moses asks them to see the hidden side of the story. In all their complaining and unbelief, someone had been carrying them.

“As a man carries his son.” It is a tender picture of a father carrying a child too small or too tired to walk. It is not the image of a general leading an army. It is the image of a parent who picks up a child, who does not shame them for being weak, and who brings them all the way home.

“All the way that you went until you came to this place.” The carrying was not occasional but constant. Every step of the forty years was a step taken with God’s help. The place where they stood was the result of his faithfulness and not their strength.

For the Christian, the verse is an assurance. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). The Father who carried Israel carries his children still, through the Son who bore our sins.
weekInReview: This week you came to the end of the book of Numbers and the beginning of Deuteronomy. You read about the sin at Baal of Peor and the zeal of Phinehas, the new census that confirmed God’s word about the old generation, and the daughters of Zelophehad, who asked for an inheritance by faith. You read of Joshua’s commissioning, the calendar of offerings, the war against Midian, and the request of the eastern tribes. You read the travel record of the forty-two stages and the boundaries of the land. You learned of the cities of refuge and the death of the high priest that sets the manslayer free. Then Moses began his sermons on the plains of Moab, looking back over the journey and reminding the new generation that God had carried them. The week taught that God keeps his word in judgment and in promise, and that he is the one who carries his people.
reflectionQuestions: Moses says that God carried Israel “as a man carries his son.” Where have you seen God carry you in a time you were not aware of it, and what would it mean to thank him for it?
The manslayer was freed by the death of the high priest. How does this picture deepen your understanding of what Christ’s death accomplished?
Moses recalled the past honestly, including his own failure. What do you need to remember honestly about your own journey, and how might that help you trust God for the future?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for carrying you when you did not know it.
Ask him to help you remember his faithfulness.
Rest in him, trusting him for the road ahead.
